The Lord Magistrate, a man whose jowls quivered with every indignant breath, seemed to be enjoying himself immensely, which was never a promising sign for the accused. For his own part, Fenn wished only for the entire farcical affair to be concluded, even if it meant a swift introduction to the city’s executioner, a man known for his regrettable lack of conversation. The banquet had been a brief, glittering affair, a final meal of such exquisite quality it felt like a deliberate cruelty, and now they were returned to the Hall of Judgment. The assembled nobles, their bellies full and their minds thirsty for spectacle, settled into their carved chairs like vultures roosting for the night. Only two figures seemed immune to the post-prandial good humor: the Lord Magistrate, whose face had soured as if he had swallowed a lemon whole, and the Silent Princess, enthroned beside him, a creature of silk and shadow who observed the proceedings from behind a beaded veil. She had not spoken a word all night; indeed, some whispered she had not spoken a word in years, but her stillness was more potent than any declaration. The Magistrate cleared his throat, a sound like gravel being churned in a bucket, and gestured for the clerk to begin. “The prisoner is charged with high treason, sedition, and the unauthorized practice of alchemy,” the clerk recited in a reedy monotone, his eyes darting nervously toward the accused. Master Fenn, standing unbound between two guards who smelled faintly of garlic and dread, offered a small, polite bow. “A busy afternoon, it would seem,” he remarked cheerfully; “one wonders how I found the time.” “Silence, sorcerer!” bellowed the Magistrate, his face turning a fascinating shade of puce. “You will answer the questions put to you, and nothing more! Your name is Fenn, is it not?” “It is the name I currently favor, my lord. It has a pleasingly earthy quality, don't you find?” A ripple of smothered laughter went through the court, which was promptly quashed by a single, murderous glare from the Magistrate. “You were discovered in the West Tower, mixing potions in brazen defiance of the royal edict!” “I was endeavoring to cure a particularly stubborn case of mildew on the tapestries, my lord, a service for which the crown ought to thank me. The smell was truly offensive!” “The ‘mildew cure’ you were brewing contained nightshade, powdered bone, and silver nitrate! These are not the components of a household cleanser!” the Magistrate roared, spittle flying from his lips. “Ah, but that is where you mistake the art of it!” Fenn replied, with the earnest air of a lecturer. “A truly persistent mildew requires a firm hand. You cannot reason with fungus, my lord; you must intimidate it!” The Magistrate seemed on the verge of an apoplexy, his hands clenching and unclenching on the arms of his throne. He looked to the Silent Princess, as if for support, but her veiled visage offered nothing, no condemnation, no approval, nothing but a consuming, absolute stillness. “You mock this court, and you mock the authority of the crown! You are a poisoner and a charlatan!” “I am a chemist, my lord, which is a very different thing. A poisoner seeks to end life; a chemist merely seeks to understand it, and occasionally, to make it more interesting. For instance,” Fenn continued, gesturing to the Magistrate, “I could devise a tincture that would cure your lordship’s unfortunate complexion in a matter of hours!” The Magistrate shot to his feet, his chair scraping loudly on the marble floor. “That is enough! You have confessed to your crimes by your own arrogant tongue! The penalty for treasonous alchemy is fixed. Clerk, prepare the warrant for beheading!” “Beheading? Oh, that seems rather drastic for an issue of household maintenance,” Fenn said with a sigh. “Could we not settle on a fine, or perhaps a sternly worded letter?” The clerk, a skeletal man with the enthusiasm of a gravedigger, was already scratching away on a sheet of parchment, which he then passed to the Magistrate for his seal. “With this warrant, your insolent ramblings will be silenced forever!” the Magistrate snarled, pressing his signet ring into the hot wax. He then held the document out for the princess to affirm. A page in livery took the parchment and knelt before the silent figure. The court held its breath. The princess did not move for a long moment; then, a single, slender hand, pale as bone and laden with silver rings, emerged from the folds of her silk robes. But she did not take the warrant. Instead, she raised one finger and beckoned to the prisoner. The guards hesitated, looking to the Magistrate, whose face was a mask of confusion. “What is the meaning of this? Her highness has no say in matters of law!” he sputtered, his authority draining away before his very eyes. The princess ignored him. Her finger remained extended, a silent, unyielding command. With a shrug, Fenn ambled forward, stopping a respectful distance from her throne. The scent of jasmine and old paper emanated from behind her veil. For the first time that night, she spoke, her voice a low, melodic whisper that carried to every corner of the silent hall. “You said you can make things more interesting. My lord Magistrate has become profoundly dull. Can you devise a tincture for that?” The Magistrate stared, his mouth agape like a landed fish. Fenn considered the question with a thoughtful frown, stroking his chin. “For a condition so advanced, your highness? It would be a challenge,” he said at last. “But I do believe it is within the realm of possibility. It would, however, require a great deal of my time, and a fully stocked laboratory.” The princess gave a single, slow nod, a gesture of finality. “Then you shall have it. Guards, escort the chemist to the Alchemist’s Spire. His work begins at dawn. Take the Lord Magistrate to his chambers; he appears to be unwell.” And with a soft rustle of silk, she rose and glided from the room, leaving behind a stunned court, a fuming magistrate being led away in disgrace, and Master Fenn, who, for the second time that evening, found himself quite surprised to still be alive.

He cast one final, lingering look at the queen, whose face remained a mask of beautiful indifference, and then he was marched from the great hall, his footsteps echoing on the marble, a sound that seemed to measure out the last few paces of his life.

The moment the door closed behind him, the fragile truce in the chamber shattered. His highness, who had been swelling with a rage that turned his already florid complexion to the color of a pickled beet, finally exploded. “You dare!” he shrieked, his voice cracking like a whip. “You dare to countermand my order! In my own court!” He took a step toward the dais, his small body trembling with a fury that was at once both terrible and ridiculous. “He was mine! His head was to be a gift to me, a bauble for my amusement!”

Queen Miranda did not flinch; she did not even appear to register his outburst for a long moment. She merely adjusted a fold in her velvet gown, a small, deliberate movement that spoke of infinite, unassailable calm. When at last she lifted her eyes to his, they were not fiery, as they had been a moment before, but as cold and as devoid of light as the bottom of a well. “Your court, you say?” she asked, her voice a low murmur that was yet more chilling than his shout. “I seem to recall this being the palace of my father. I seem to recall this crown being placed upon my head. You are here, my little prince, because I suffer you to be here. Do not forget that again.”

The dwarf seemed to shrink, the hot air of his rage deflating under the icy pressure of her words. He opened his mouth, a stream of venomous protest on his lips, but the queen simply raised a single, white finger, and he fell silent. “We have other business,” she stated, not as a question, but as a fact. “You wished to see justice done, and so you shall. The Duke will call the next case. Let us be entertained.” She settled back into her throne, the very picture of regal ennui, dropping her lashes once more as if the scene had already bored her into a stupor. The message, however, was as clear as if it had been blazoned in fire across the wall; she was the master, and they were but players in her private theater.

The duke, who had been watching this exchange with the nervous attention of a man standing between two ill tempered lions, cleared his throat and hastily unrolled his scroll. “Ahem! Yes! Her majesty is correct. Let justice proceed! Guards! Bring forth the accused, the Lady Beatrice Castlemaine!” His voice trembled slightly, for he had been dealt a near miss, and he knew it. Two guards disappeared and returned in short order, leading between them a woman of striking, if somewhat faded, beauty. She was tall and slender, with hair the color of spun moonlight piled high on her head, though several strands had escaped to trail distractedly about her pale face. Her eyes, wide and blue, were filled with a terror so profound it seemed to have scoured all other expression from her features. She stumbled as they brought her before the green table, and would have fallen had not one of the guards caught her arm.

“Lady Castlemaine,” the duke began, his judicial severity returning now that the immediate danger to his own person had passed, “you stand accused of a most heinous crime. The poisoning of her grace, the Duchess of Sutherland. What have you to say for yourself?” The lady shook her head, her lips moving but no sound coming out. She looked wildly from the duke to the grinning face of the dwarf, and finally, desperately, to the still, silent form of the queen. “Your majesty,” she whispered, her voice a mere thread of sound. “I am innocent. I swear it.”

“Innocence is a luxury we can seldom afford in this court, my dear,” cackled his highness, leaning so far forward he nearly toppled from his chair. “But we are willing to be convinced. Tell us your story. Make it amusing, and perhaps we shall only have you whipped.” A ripple of nervous laughter went through the assembled nobles, a sound that died instantly as the queen shifted in her seat.

Let us investigate them.” Her eyes, still hidden behind her lashes, seemed nonetheless to be fixed upon the duke, who flinched as if she had struck him. “Indeed, your majesty,” he said quickly. “There is a witness. A certain maidservant from the duchess’s own household.” He snapped his fingers, and a small, trembling girl in a plain brown frock was pushed forward by a guard. She was no more than sixteen, and she kept her eyes fixed on the floor, twisting the hem of her apron in her hands.

I dare not.” His highness slammed a tiny fist on the table. “You will dare, or you will find yourself in a place that makes Lady Castlemaine’s predicament seem a pleasant holiday! Now, speak!”

Thus encouraged, the girl took a ragged breath and began to stammer out her tale. She spoke of seeing Lady Castlemaine coming from the duchess’s chambers late at night, of a small vial clutched in her ladyship’s hand, of the duchess’s cries of pain an hour later. It was a simple, damning story, and with every word, the color drained further from Lady Castlemaine’s face. When the girl had finished, there was a profound silence in the room. The duke looked triumphant; the dwarf looked ecstatic. “Well,” his highness said, rubbing his hands together. “That seems quite conclusive. I believe we are ready to pronounce sentence.”

“No!” Lady Castlemaine suddenly found her voice, and it was a shriek of pure desperation. “She lies! It is all a lie!” “And why should she lie, my lady?” the duke asked, with a smug, condescending smile. “What reason would a simple serving girl have to invent such a tale against a person of your rank?” “Because she was paid to!” Lady Castlemaine cried, pointing a shaking finger not at the maid, but at the duke himself. “Paid by you! You, who desired the duchess’s lands for your own! You, who promised me advancement at court if I would but help you remove her!”

The duke turned a shade of purple so deep it was nearly black. “This is outrageous! An absurd accusation from a condemned murderess!” he spluttered. But his eyes darted nervously toward the queen, and a number of the other nobles began to murmur amongst themselves. The accusation, fantastic as it was, had the uncomfortable ring of truth to it, for the duke’s avarice was legendary. His highness, Prince Caliban, was beside himself with glee. A simple execution was one thing; but a scandal that implicated one of his chief ministers was a far richer entertainment. “Oh, this is wonderful!” he chortled. “A plot within a plot! My lord duke, I do hope you have a better defense than simple indignation!”

All eyes turned now to the queen. She had not moved, had not given any sign that she was even listening. But now, she slowly, deliberately, lifted her head, and her dark eyes, no longer veiled, swept the room. They rested for a moment on the terrified maid, on the desperate Lady Castlemaine, on the apoplectic duke, and finally on her grinning consort. “The maid,” the queen said, her voice cutting through the babble. “Bring her here.”

The guard propelled the trembling Annie forward until she stood at the very foot of the throne. The queen leaned forward slightly, and the girl flinched as if expecting a blow. “Look at me, child,” Miranda commanded, and her tone was not unkind. Reluctantly, Annie lifted her tear-stained face. “You say you saw a vial in Lady Castlemaine’s hand. Describe it.” “It was… it was small, your majesty. And dark. Made of blue glass, with a silver stopper.” “A silver stopper,” the queen repeated, thoughtfully. She turned her gaze to Lady Castlemaine. “My lady, do you possess such a vial?” “Never, your majesty! I swear it!”

The queen then looked at the duke. “My lord duke. You are a man of some learning. A student of the arcane arts, I am told.” The duke’s eyes widened. “A mere hobby, your majesty. Trifles.” “Trifles, of course,” the queen agreed, a faint, dangerous smile touching her lips for the first time. “And in your collection of trifles, do you happen to have a small vial of blue glass, with a silver stopper, perhaps containing a rare poison from the eastern continent, a poison that mimics the effects of a sudden, violent ague?”

The duke’s face, which had been purple with rage, now became as white as bleached bone. He took a half-step back, his mouth opening and closing like a fish. The entire court held its breath. The silence was absolute. “I see,” the queen said at last, her voice soft as silk. “You need not answer. Your face has answered for you.” She rose to her feet in a single, fluid motion, a column of velvet and ice. “It seems we have misidentified the murderer. Lady Castlemaine is guilty only of ambition and profound foolishness in choosing her conspirators. For that, she will be exiled. A dreary, but survivable, fate. The serving girl lied, under duress, and shall be sent to a nunnery where she may contemplate the virtue of truth. But you, my lord duke,” and here her eyes narrowed, “you have not only attempted murder, but you have attempted to make a mockery of my court and my justice. For that, there can be only one penalty.”

She looked over at the dwarf, who was staring, for once, in stunned silence. “His highness was promised a beheading tonight,” she said, her voice ringing with finality. “And a beheading he shall have. Just not the one he was expecting. Guards, seize the duke. Let him be prepared alongside the other prisoner. Their executions will proceed together, at dawn.” And with that, she swept from the room, her silken train whispering over the marble floor, leaving behind a scene of utter chaos and disbelief, with the duke shrieking for mercy as he was dragged away by the same guards who, not ten minutes prior, had been his loyal servants.

The dungeon to which he had been consigned was a dungeon of the truest sort, a place of weeping stone and the scent of ages of despair, where the very air was a thick, damp blanket against the lungs. Chained to the wall, with nothing but a pile of rank straw for a bed, he had ample time for the reflections he had been so impatient to avoid. His case was indeed desperate; he had insulted a prince, defied a queen, and confessed to killing a nobleman, highwayman or not. There was no appeal, no hope of rescue. He was to die at dawn, a fact that had been a comfort in its certainty but was now, in the waiting, a source of slow, creeping dread.

He could hear, faintly, the sounds from the great hall above; a shriek, a roar of laughter, a sudden, ringing silence. It was the sound of the strange, mad court continuing its business, and he found himself wondering about the fate of the next poor soul on the docket, the Lady Castlemaine. He thought, too, of the queen. That strange, cold, beautiful woman, who had seemed as bored by signing his death warrant as she might be by any other trivial household task. The memory of her fair hand, scrawling his doom, still sent a sharp, inexplicable pang through his heart. It was not love, nor was it fear; it was a profound, frustrating confusion. He could not understand her, and for a man like Sir Norman, who prided himself on his judgment of character, this was the most galling fact of all.

Hours passed. The faint sounds from above had ceased, and a deeper silence had fallen over the palace, broken only by the drip, drip, drip of water somewhere in the darkness of his cell. He must have dozed, for he was startled awake by the sound of a key turning in the heavy lock of his door. He struggled to his feet, the chains rattling, his heart pounding a sudden, frantic rhythm against his ribs. Was it dawn already? Had his time come so soon?

The door swung inward with a groan of protest, and a sliver of light from a lantern sliced through the oppressive gloom. It was not the headsman, however, nor was it the guards who had brought him here. The figure in the doorway was small and slight, wrapped in a dark cloak, one of the queen’s gauzy nymphs from the court above. It was the same one, he realized, who had presented the vellum to the queen for her signature. She carried the lantern in one hand, and a small tray in the other, on which sat a loaf of bread, a piece of cheese, and a flask of wine. She stepped inside, and the door swung shut behind her, plunging them back into near darkness, save for the small, golden circle of the lantern’s light.

“Her majesty thought you might be hungry,” the girl whispered, her voice trembling. She set the tray down on a stone ledge, well out of his reach. Sir Norman stared at her, dumbfounded. “Her majesty?” he repeated, his voice hoarse. “The same majesty who signed my death warrant sends me dinner? Is this another of this court’s peculiar jests?” The girl shook her head, her eyes wide in the flickering light. “The queen’s motives are her own,” she said, reciting the words as if from memory. “She bids me tell you that she sees more than she pretends to see. She knows you are no common spy, and that the man you shot was indeed a brigand in the duke’s employ.”

Sir Norman’s mind reeled. “If she knows this, then why…?” “The duke was a fool, but a powerful one,” the girl interrupted, her fear giving way to a strange, knowing confidence. “His fall had to be arranged. Your arrival was… opportune. You provided the means.” “A means to what?” Sir Norman demanded. “A pawn in some game I do not understand? And what now? Am I to be executed alongside this disgraced duke to tie up all the loose ends?”

The girl looked at him, and for a moment, he thought he saw a flicker of pity in her eyes. “The queen’s game is long, and its rules are known only to her. Your fate, Sir Norman, is not as certain as you believe. The execution is set for dawn. But dawn is still some hours away.” She picked up her lantern and moved back to the door. “What does that mean?” he called after her. “What am I to do?” She paused in the doorway, her face half in shadow. “The queen rewards those who are useful to her,” she said softly. “And she has a great appreciation for those who can create their own opportunities.” Then she was gone, and the lock turned once more, leaving him alone in the absolute darkness, with the scent of bread and wine, and a single, bewildering spark of hope, more terrifying in its way than the certainty of death had ever been.

Made of blue glass, with a silver stopper.” “A silver stopper,” the queen repeated, thoughtfully. She turned her gaze to Lady Castlemaine. “My lady, do you possess such a vial?” “Never, your majesty! I swear it!”

The queen then looked at the duke. “My lord duke. You are a man of some learning. A student of the arcane arts, I am told.” The duke’s eyes widened. “A mere hobby, your majesty. Trifles.” “Trifles, of course,” the queen agreed, a faint, dangerous smile touching her lips for the first time. “And in your collection of trifles, do you happen to have a small vial of blue glass, with a silver stopper, perhaps containing a rare poison from the eastern continent, a poison that mimics the effects of a sudden, violent ague?”

The duke’s face, which had been purple with rage, now became as white as bleached bone. He took a half-step back, his mouth opening and closing like a fish. The entire court held its breath. But you, my lord duke,” and here her eyes narrowed, “you have not only attempted murder, but you have attempted to make a mockery of my court and my justice. For that, there can be only one penalty.”

She looked over at the dwarf, who was staring, for once, in stunned silence. “His highness was promised a beheading tonight,” she said, her voice ringing with finality. “And a beheading he shall have. Their executions will proceed together, at dawn.” And with that, she swept from the room, her silken train whispering over the marble floor, leaving behind a scene of utter chaos and disbelief, with the duke shrieking for mercy as he was dragged away by the same guards who, not ten minutes prior, had been his loyal servants.

Chained to the wall, with nothing but a pile of rank straw for a bed, he had ample time for the reflections he had been so impatient to avoid. His case was indeed desperate; he had insulted a prince, defied a queen, and confessed to killing a nobleman, highwayman or not. There was no appeal, no hope of rescue. He was to die at dawn, a fact that had been a comfort in its certainty but was now, in the waiting, a source of slow, creeping dread.

He could hear, faintly, the sounds from the great hall above; a shriek, a roar of laughter, a sudden, ringing silence. It was the sound of the strange, mad court continuing its business, and he found himself wondering about the fate of the next poor soul on the docket, the Lady Castlemaine. He thought, too, of the queen. That strange, cold, beautiful woman, who had seemed as bored by signing his death warrant as she might be by any other trivial household task. The memory of her fair hand, scrawling his doom, still sent a sharp, inexplicable pang through his heart. It was not love, nor was it fear; it was a profound, frustrating confusion. He could not understand her, and for a man like Sir Norman, who prided himself on his judgment of character, this was the most galling fact of all.

He must have dozed, for he was startled awake by the sound of a key turning in the heavy lock of his door. He struggled to his feet, the chains rattling, his heart pounding a sudden, frantic rhythm against his ribs. Was it dawn already? Had his time come so soon?

The door swung inward with a groan of protest, and a sliver of light from a lantern sliced through the oppressive gloom. It was not the headsman, however, nor was it the guards who had brought him here. The figure in the doorway was small and slight, wrapped in a dark cloak, one of the queen’s gauzy nymphs from the court above. It was the same one, he realized, who had presented the vellum to the queen for her signature. She carried the lantern in one hand, and a small tray in the other, on which sat a loaf of bread, a piece of cheese, and a flask of wine. She stepped inside, and the door swung shut behind her, plunging them back into near darkness, save for the small, golden circle of the lantern’s light.

“Her majesty thought you might be hungry,” the girl whispered, her voice trembling. She set the tray down on a stone ledge, well out of his reach. Sir Norman stared at her, dumbfounded. “Her majesty?” he repeated, his voice hoarse. “The same majesty who signed my death warrant sends me dinner? Is this another of this court’s peculiar jests?” The girl shook her head, her eyes wide in the flickering light. “The queen’s motives are her own,” she said, reciting the words as if from memory. “She bids me tell you that she sees more than she pretends to see. She knows you are no common spy, and that the man you shot was indeed a brigand in the duke’s employ.”

Sir Norman’s mind reeled. “If she knows this, then why…?” “The duke was a fool, but a powerful one,” the girl interrupted, her fear giving way to a strange, knowing confidence. “His fall had to be arranged. Your arrival was… opportune. You provided the means.” “A means to what?” Sir Norman demanded. “A pawn in some game I do not understand? And what now? Am I to be executed alongside this disgraced duke to tie up all the loose ends?”

The girl looked at him, and for a moment, he thought he saw a flicker of pity in her eyes. “The queen’s game is long, and its rules are known only to her. Your fate, Sir Norman, is not as certain as you believe. The execution is set for dawn. But dawn is still some hours away.” She picked up her lantern and moved back to the door. “What does that mean?” he called after her. “What am I to do?” She paused in the doorway, her face half in shadow. “The queen rewards those who are useful to her,” she said softly. “And she has a great appreciation for those who can create their own opportunities.” Then she was gone, and the lock turned once more, leaving him alone in the absolute darkness, with the scent of bread and wine, and a single, bewildering spark of hope, more terrifying in its way than the certainty of death had ever been.

He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, a look of satisfaction spreading across his coarse features. “Her majesty keeps a good cellar, I’ll give her that,” he said, then took another, deeper drink. He turned to leave, and as he did, his steps seemed to falter. He put a hand to his head, a puzzled expression on his face. “Strange… very dizzy, all of a sudden…”

Sir Norman held his breath. The nymph’s words about the queen seeing more than she pretended came back to him. Had she known this would happen? Had the wine been drugged not with poison, but with a powerful soporific?

The guard took another stumbling step towards the door, then his eyes rolled back in his head, and he collapsed to the stone floor with a crash that echoed like a thunderclap in the confined space. He was as still and silent as a felled ox.

For a moment, Sir Norman could only stare. The sheer, improbable success of his gambit left him stunned. But there was no time for astonishment. The noise of the guard’s fall might have been heard. He shuffled as far as his chains would allow, his boots scraping on the stone, and stretched his body to its absolute limit. His fingers brushed against the guard’s tunic, searching frantically. He found a large iron ring heavy with keys.

His hands trembled as he sorted through them, the clinking of the metal deafeningly loud. He tried one key, then another, in the locks on his wrists. The third one turned with a smooth, satisfying click. The iron band fell away from his right wrist. Freedom! He quickly unlocked the other, his heart hammering against his ribs as if it meant to break free.

He was standing, unbound, in the center of the cell, a free man, if a man could be called free in the heart of his enemy’s fortress. He stripped the sleeping guard of his sword and belt, and a dagger from his boot. Armed, he felt a measure of his old self-assurance return. He picked up the lantern, its light a precious beacon, and slipped out of the cell, pulling the heavy door shut behind him.

He was in a long, narrow corridor hewn from the living rock, lined with doors identical to his own. The air was thick with the smell of mildew and despair. Faintly, from far above, he could hear the muffled echo of voices and a sudden, sharp cry. The trial of Lady Castlemaine must be underway.

Following the sounds, he moved cautiously through the labyrinthine passages of the dungeon. The architecture was a confusing maze, designed, no doubt, to confound escapees, but the intermittent sounds from the court above served as his compass. He ascended a winding flight of stone stairs, the voices growing clearer. He emerged into a small, dark antechamber, separated from the main hall by a heavy tapestry. Peering through a small gap in the weave, he found he had a clear, if narrow, view of the proceedings.

The scene was much as he had left it, though the central figures had changed. In the prisoner’s stand was a woman of extraordinary beauty, her face a mask of pale, defiant fury. This, he surmised, must be Lady Castlemaine. She stood tall and unbowed, her magnificent gown of sapphire silk a stark contrast to her grim surroundings, her hands bound before her with a golden cord.

The duke, who had condemned him with such relish, now sat beside his highness the dwarf, but his aspect was greatly changed. His face was ashen, his judicial dignity utterly vanished, replaced by a twitching, rodent-like nervousness. He kept glancing at the queen, who sat in her high-backed chair, as still and remote as a marble effigy, her expression unreadable.

“You deny, then, my lady,” the dwarf was saying, his voice dripping with mock sympathy, “that you procured a rare poison from the East, known as the Serpent’s Kiss?”

“I deny everything,” Lady Castlemaine snapped, her voice clear and ringing with contempt. “This entire proceeding is a farce, orchestrated by a jumped-up jester and a coward!” She shot a look of pure venom at the duke, who flinched as if struck.

“A coward he may be,” chirped the dwarf, grinning, “but he is the one who brought your treason to our attention. Is that not so, your grace?”

All eyes turned to the duke. He swallowed hard, his jowls trembling. “It is so, your highness. I… I had my suspicions. I observed her ladyship meeting with a suspicious apothecary. I feared for the safety of the court… for her majesty’s safety above all!”

A low murmur went through the assembled nobles. Sir Norman watched, fascinated. The duke was clearly trying to ingratiate himself with the queen, to salvage his position by sacrificing this woman.

“Indeed?” the queen’s voice cut through the air, cool and sharp as an icicle. It was the first time she had spoken. “You were concerned for my safety, duke? How very thoughtful. And yet, was not this Duchess of Sutherland, the supposed victim, your own cousin?”

The duke turned a shade of mottled purple. “Majesty, my loyalty to the crown supersedes all familial bonds! When I discovered the plot…”

“What plot?” Lady Castlemaine interrupted, laughing a bitter, incredulous laugh. “There was no plot! You gave me the vial yourself, you sniveling worm! You told me it was for the queen!”

A collective gasp went through the hall. The duke leaped to his feet, his face a mask of horror. “Lies! Slander! She is mad! She seeks to drag me down with her!”

“Did he now?” the queen said, her voice dangerously soft. She leaned forward just slightly, and the movement seemed to draw all the energy in the room towards her. “He told you the poison was for me? And you, my dear Lady Castlemaine, you agreed to administer it? For what price? His love? Or a place by his side when he took my throne?”

Lady Castlemaine’s defiance finally crumbled. A tear traced a path through the powder on her cheek. “He promised me… he said you were a tyrant, a witch… that the kingdom suffered under your cold hand. He said he would be a better ruler, a kinder one.”

“Silence her!” the duke shrieked, his composure completely shattered. “She is a lying traitor!”

“Oh, I have no doubt she is a traitor,” the queen said, her eyes, cold and dark, now fixed upon the duke. “But I am beginning to think she was merely your tool. A rather foolish and ambitious one, but a tool nonetheless. You, on the other hand, duke… you seem to be the craftsman of this entire affair.”

She made a slight, elegant gesture with her hand. “You accuse her of poisoning your cousin. She accuses you of plotting to poison me. And a few hours ago, you brought me a captured ‘spy,’ whom you accused of murdering your compatriot, Lord Ashley.” She paused, letting the words hang in the air. “It has been a very busy night for you. A night of tying up loose ends, perhaps?”

The duke stood frozen, his mouth opening and closing like a landed fish. His highness the dwarf was watching the exchange with rapt, malicious glee, his head turning from the duke to the queen as if he were at a tennis match.

“You see,” the queen continued, her voice resonating with cold authority, “I, too, have my little spies. And they tell me that Lord Ashley was no lord, but a common cut-throat in your employ. They tell me he was your agent in a great many dirty deeds. And they tell me that your meeting with him on the road tonight was not to apprehend a spy, but to finalize a bargain with emissaries from my dear cousin, Charles.”

The room was utterly silent. The duke’s face had gone from purple to a ghastly, pasty white. He looked like a man who had just seen his own grave dug before him.

“You sought to sell this kingdom,” the queen declared, her voice rising, yet losing none of its icy control. “And to clear the way, you intended to remove me. Lady Castlemaine was to be your assassin, and Sir Norman Kingsley, the convenient scapegoat, a royalist spy caught in the act of murder, whose execution would serve as a fine distraction. She rose to her feet, a figure of terrible, beautiful majesty. “Your plot to kill me with poison is treason. Your conspiracy with the enemies of this realm is treason. Your murder of your own agent, Lord Ashley, which you sought to lay at another’s door, reveals you as a man without honor. You have, in a single night, proven yourself unfit to live.” She turned to the guards. “Seize him.”

The duke gave a strangled cry of terror and outrage as the soldiers moved forward. He made a desperate, lurching motion, not to fight, but to flee, and in his panic, he knocked over the small table beside him. A roll of vellum, the one he had been scrawling on earlier, fell to the floor and rolled towards the tapestry where Sir Norman was hiding.

Instinctively, Sir Norman stooped and picked it up. It was another death warrant. But the name written upon it was not his, nor was it Lady Castlemaine’s. In the duke’s spidery, agitated hand was written: “His Royal Highness, Prince Caliban.”

Understanding struck Sir Norman with the force of a physical blow. The dwarf! The duke’s final, desperate move was to have been the elimination of his diminutive partner in crime.

At that moment, the guards seized the duke, hauling him, struggling and screaming, before the queen. And in the commotion, the dwarf, his sharp eyes missing nothing, saw the tapestry move. He saw the hand retrieve the vellum. His grin vanished, replaced by a look of cunning suspicion.

“There is someone behind the arras!” he screeched, pointing a long, bony finger.

Every head in the room turned. Two guards immediately moved toward the tapestry. There was no escape. Taking a deep breath, Sir Norman pushed the heavy fabric aside and stepped out into the light, the vellum still in his hand.

A collective gasp went up. He stood there, sword at his hip, lantern in hand, no longer a condemned prisoner but a grim, armed specter from the dungeons. The queen’s eyes widened, but only for an instant. A slow, knowing smile, the first real smile he had seen from her, touched her lips. It was not a warm smile; it was the smile of a chess master who sees her opponent walk directly into her final, exquisite checkmate.

“Sir Norman Kingsley,” she said, her voice smooth as silk. “It seems the reports of your incarceration were exaggerated. You have, it appears, created an opportunity for yourself. And you have brought us a gift, I see.”

Sir Norman walked forward, his boots echoing in the stunned silence. He ignored the gaping nobles and the furious, sputtering dwarf. He walked directly to the foot of the queen’s dais, knelt on one knee, and offered her the roll of vellum.

“Your majesty,” he said, his voice steady. “I believe this belongs to you.”

She took it from him, her cool fingers brushing his. She unrolled it, read the name, and then looked at the dwarf. His highness Prince Caliban was no longer grinning. For the first time, his grotesque face was a mask of pure, unadulterated fear.

“Well, well,” the queen murmured, a sound like the rustling of dry leaves. “It seems our duke was a more ambitious traitor than even I had supposed. He meant to have not only my throne, but my consort’s life as well.” She tossed the vellum onto the table. “Guards, you have two prisoners for the Black Chamber now instead of one. Take the duke away. And Lady Castlemaine… your foolishness has saved you. You will be confined to the Grey Tower for the rest of your days. Be grateful it is not a headstone.”

As the weeping lady and the shrieking duke were dragged from the hall, the queen’s gaze returned to Sir Norman, still kneeling before her. The room was quiet, the remaining nobles watching with breathless anticipation.

“You have done me a service tonight, Sir Norman,” she said, her voice once again cool and distant. “Two services, in fact. You rid me of a troublesome highwayman, and you have exposed a far more dangerous traitor in our midst. Such service requires a reward.” She paused. “I cannot let it be known that I pardon a man condemned as a spy, for my justice must appear implacable. And I cannot let you go, for you know too much.”

Sir Norman’s heart sank. Had he escaped the axe only to find a subtler, more permanent prison?

“Therefore,” she continued, a flicker of something unreadable in her dark eyes, “your sentence stands. Sir Norman Kingsley died in the dungeons tonight, a condemned spy. But from the dungeons, a new man has emerged, a man who knows how to seize his chances. A man who might be… useful. You are a skilled swordsman, are you not?”

“I have some small reputation, majesty,” he replied, his mind racing.

“Then you shall have a new name, and a new post. Henceforth, you are Captain Valerius, of my personal guard. Your life is mine. Your sword is mine. You will see what I wish you to see, and you will be blind to all else. You will speak when I bid you, and you will be silent as the grave otherwise. You are no longer a knight of King Charles; you are a shadow in my court. Do you accept these terms?”

It was not freedom. It was a gilded cage, a life sentence of service to this terrifying, brilliant, and inscrutable woman. But it was life. It was a chance. It was the only move left on the board.

He raised his head and met her gaze without flinching. “I accept, your majesty.”

“Good,” she said, and for the second time, she smiled that thin, sharp smile. “Rise, Captain Valerius. Your watch begins now.”

The guard grunted in agreement, pulling the stopper from the flask and taking a long, gurgling swallow. He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, a look of satisfaction spreading across his coarse features. “Her majesty keeps a good cellar, I’ll give her that,” he said, then took another, deeper drink. He picked up the bread and cheese as well, tucking them into his tunic. “A pity for you, I suppose. But a good turn for me.”

He shuffled as far as his chains would allow, his boots scraping on the stone, and stretched his body to its absolute limit. His fingers brushed against the guard’s tunic, searching frantically. He found a large iron ring heavy with keys.

His hands trembled as he sorted through them, the clinking of the metal deafeningly loud. He tried one key, then another, in the locks on his wrists. The third one turned with a smooth, satisfying click. The iron band fell away from his right wrist. Freedom! He quickly unlocked the other, his heart hammering against his ribs as if it meant to break free.

He was standing, unbound, in the center of the cell, a free man, if a man could be called free in the heart of his enemy’s fortress. He stripped the sleeping guard of his sword and belt, and a dagger from his boot. Armed, he felt a measure of his old self-assurance return. He picked up the lantern, its light a precious beacon, and slipped out of the cell, pulling the heavy door shut behind him.

He was in a long, narrow corridor hewn from the living rock, lined with doors identical to his own. The air was thick with the smell of mildew and despair. Faintly, from far above, he could hear the muffled echo of voices and a sudden, sharp cry. The trial of Lady Castlemaine must be underway.

The architecture was a confusing maze, designed, no doubt, to confound escapees, but the intermittent sounds from the court above served as his compass. He ascended a winding flight of stone stairs, the voices growing clearer. He emerged into a small, dark antechamber, separated from the main hall by a heavy tapestry. Peering through a small gap in the weave, he found he had a clear, if narrow, view of the proceedings.

The scene was much as he had left it, though the central figures had changed. In the prisoner’s stand was a woman of extraordinary beauty, her face a mask of pale, defiant fury. This, he surmised, must be Lady Castlemaine. She stood tall and unbowed, her magnificent gown of sapphire silk a stark contrast to her grim surroundings, her hands bound before her with a golden cord.

The duke, who had condemned him with such relish, now sat beside his highness the dwarf, but his aspect was greatly changed. His face was ashen, his judicial dignity utterly vanished, replaced by a twitching, rodent-like nervousness. He kept glancing at the queen, who sat in her high-backed chair, as still and remote as a marble effigy, her expression unreadable.

The duke turned a shade of mottled purple. “Majesty, my loyalty to the crown supersedes all familial bonds! When I discovered the plot…”

A collective gasp went through the hall. The duke leaped to his feet, his face a mask of horror. “Lies! Slander! She is mad! She seeks to drag me down with her!”

“Did he now?” the queen said, her voice dangerously soft. She leaned forward just slightly, and the movement seemed to draw all the energy in the room towards her. “He told you the poison was for me? They tell me he was your agent in a great many dirty deeds. The room was utterly silent. The duke’s face had gone from purple to a ghastly, pasty white. He looked like a man who had just seen his own grave dug before him.

Your murder of your own agent, Lord Ashley, which you sought to lay at another’s door, reveals you as a man without honor. You have, in a single night, proven yourself unfit to live.” She turned to the guards. “Seize him.”

He made a desperate, lurching motion, not to fight, but to flee, and in his panic, he knocked over the small table beside him. A roll of vellum, the one he had been scrawling on earlier, fell to the floor and rolled towards the tapestry where Sir Norman was hiding.

Instinctively, Sir Norman stooped and picked it up. It was another death warrant. But the name written upon it was not his, nor was it Lady Castlemaine’s. In the duke’s spidery, agitated hand was written: “His Royal Highness, Prince Caliban.”

Understanding struck Sir Norman with the force of a physical blow. The dwarf! The duke’s final, desperate move was to have been the elimination of his diminutive partner in crime.

At that moment, the guards seized the duke, hauling him, struggling and screaming, before the queen. And in the commotion, the dwarf, his sharp eyes missing nothing, saw the tapestry move. He saw the hand retrieve the vellum. His grin vanished, replaced by a look of cunning suspicion.

“There is someone behind the arras!” he screeched, pointing a long, bony finger.

Every head in the room turned. Two guards immediately moved toward the tapestry. There was no escape. Taking a deep breath, Sir Norman pushed the heavy fabric aside and stepped out into the light, the vellum still in his hand.

The queen’s eyes widened, but only for an instant. A slow, knowing smile, the first real smile he had seen from her, touched her lips. She took it from him, her cool fingers brushing his. She unrolled it, read the name, and then looked at the dwarf. His highness Prince Caliban was no longer grinning. For the first time, his grotesque face was a mask of pure, unadulterated fear.

As the weeping lady and the shrieking duke were dragged from the hall, the queen’s gaze returned to Sir Norman, still kneeling before her. The room was quiet, the remaining nobles watching with breathless anticipation.

“You have done me a service tonight, Sir Norman,” she said, her voice once again cool and distant. “Two services, in fact. You rid me of a troublesome highwayman, and you have exposed a far more dangerous traitor in our midst. Such service requires a reward.” She paused. “I cannot let it be known that I pardon a man condemned as a spy, for my justice must appear implacable. And I cannot let you go, for you know too much.”

Sir Norman’s heart sank. Had he escaped the axe only to find a subtler, more permanent prison?

“Therefore,” she continued, a flicker of something unreadable in her dark eyes, “your sentence stands. Sir Norman Kingsley died in the dungeons tonight, a condemned spy. But from the dungeons, a new man has emerged, a man who knows how to seize his chances. A man who might be… useful. You are a skilled swordsman, are you not?”

“I have some small reputation, majesty,” he replied, his mind racing.

“Then you shall have a new name, and a new post. Henceforth, you are Captain Valerius, of my personal guard. Your life is mine. Your sword is mine. You will see what I wish you to see, and you will be blind to all else. You will speak when I bid you, and you will be silent as the grave otherwise. You are no longer a knight of King Charles; you are a shadow in my court. Do you accept these terms?”

It was not freedom. It was a gilded cage, a life sentence of service to this terrifying, brilliant, and inscrutable woman. But it was life. It was a chance. It was the only move left on the board.

He raised his head and met her gaze without flinching. “I accept, your majesty.”

“Good,” she said, and for the second time, she smiled that thin, sharp smile. “Rise, Captain Valerius. Your watch begins now.”
